claim: Damaraland mole-rats are frequently classified as 'eusocial'.
source: Like naked mole-rats (Heterocephalus glaber), Damaraland mole-rats are frequently classified as 'eusocial' (Bennett and Faulkes, 2000; Jarvis, 1981; Jarvis and Bennett, 1993)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bennett and Faulkes, 2000; Jarvis, 1981; Jarvis and Bennett, 1993

claim: Female helpers who transition to queens experience accelerated vertebral growth associated with increases in fecundity.
source: female helpers who transition to queens experience accelerated vertebral growth associated with increases in fecundity (O'Riain et al., 2000; Thorley et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Riain et al., 2000 and Thorley et al., 2018

claim: Queens experience vertebral growth that likely confers advantages to fecundity.
source: we confirm that queens experience vertebral growth that likely confers advantages to fecundity
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing vertebral growth in queens and correlation with fecundity

claim: Queens upregulate bone resorption pathways.
source: they also upregulate bone resorption pathways
evidence: Supported by gene expression data showing enrichment of bone resorption pathways

claim: Queens show reductions in femoral mass.
source: show reductions in femoral mass
evidence: Supported by micro-CT scan measurements of femoral cortical bone

claim: Reductions in femoral mass predict increased vulnerability to fracture in queens.
source: which predicts increased vulnerability to fracture
evidence: Based on modeling using mouse data relating cortical area to maximum load

claim: Reproductive division of labor in mole-rats leads to gene regulatory rewiring.
source: reproductive division of labor in mole-rats leads to gene regulatory rewiring
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data showing differential gene expression between queens and nonbreeders

claim: Reproductive division of labor in mole-rats leads to extensive morphological plasticity.
source: reproductive division of labor in mole-rats leads to gene regulatory rewiring and extensive morphological plasticity
evidence: Supported by x-ray and micro-CT data showing morphological differences between queens and nonbreeders

claim: Concentrated reproduction in mole-rats is accompanied by costs to bone strength.
source: in mole-rats, concentrated reproduction is also accompanied by costs to bone strength
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced cortical bone and predicted increased fracture risk

claim: Queens are frequently much larger than their sterile colony mates in eusocial insects.
source: Queens are frequently much larger than their sterile colony mates (e.g., twice as large in honey bees and Pharaoh ants; Berndt and Eichler, 1987; Page and Peng, 2001)
evidence: Supported by citations to Berndt and Eichler, 1987 and Page and Peng, 2001

claim: Dramatically altered growth and development programs in eusocial insect queens are explained by changes in gene regulation.
source: reflecting dramatically altered growth and development programs that are explained by changes in gene regulation (Smith et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al., 2008

claim: New breeders in some vertebrate species undergo a period of accelerated growth.
source: In some species, new breeders undergo a period of accelerated growth, which may be important either for maintaining dominance or for supporting high fecundity (Clutton-Brock et al., 2006; Huchard et al., 2016; O'Riain et al., 2000; Russell et al., 2004; Thorley et al., 2018; Young and Bennett, 2010)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Substantial gene regulatory divergence with breeding status has been described for the brain and some peripheral organs.
source: While substantial gene regulatory divergence with breeding status has been described for the brain and some peripheral organs (Bens et al., 2018; Mulugeta et al., 2017; Sahm et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bens et al., 2018; Mulugeta et al., 2017; Sahm et al., 2020

claim: At the time of assignment, females assigned to queen, helper, and solitaire treatments were statistically indistinguishable in body mass, age, and vertebral length.
source: At the time of assignment, females assigned to the queen, helper, and solitaire treatments were statistically indistinguishable in body mass, age, and vertebral length (as measured by LV5; unpaired t-tests between all pairwise combinations of treatments: p>0.05; Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by statistical tests and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Queens showed rapid growth in the lumbar vertebrae in the first 12 months post-pairing compared to nonbreeders.
source: Compared to nonbreeders, queens showed rapid growth in the LV in the first 12 months post-pairing (Figure 1D, E), especially in the vertebrae toward the caudal end of the vertebral column (LV5 and LV6)
evidence: Supported by longitudinal x-ray measurements shown in Figure 1D and E

claim: Most differential growth in queens was concentrated soon after the breeding status transition.
source: Based on longitudinal measurements, most of this differential growth was concentrated soon after the breeding status transition
evidence: Supported by analysis of growth rates at different time intervals

claim: There is a significant interaction between breeding status and post-pairing time point in the first four months of the experiment.
source: Specifically, we observed a significant interaction between breeding status (queen versus nonbreeder) and post-pairing time point in the first four months of the experiment (Figure 1D; β = 0.0794, p=3.13×10−3; n = 49 x-rays from 28 animals)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 1D

claim: Only queens that had already experienced pregnancy showed accelerated vertebral lengthening relative to nonbreeders in the first four months.
source: Moreover, in the first four months, only queens that had already experienced pregnancy showed accelerated vertebral lengthening relative to nonbreeders (unpaired t-test; LV5 of pregnant queens versus nonbreeders: t = −5.735, df = 16.871, p=2.50×10−5; LV5 of queens not yet pregnant versus nonbreeders: t = −0.789, df = 13.007, p=0.444; n = 14 nonbreeders, five pregnant queens, and two queens not yet pregnant)
evidence: Supported by statistical tests comparing pregnant queens, non-pregnant queens, and nonbreeders

claim: After 12 months, the absolute length of LV5 in queens was, on average, 4.8% longer than nonbreeders.
source: After 12 months, the absolute length of LV5 in queens was, on average, 4.8% longer than nonbreeders (Figure 1E; LV5: unpaired t-test, t = 2.509, df = 21.095, p=0.020)
evidence: Supported by statistical test and Figure 1E

claim: Queens with longer bodies had more pups per litter.
source: Queens with longer bodies (which correlates with longer LV, Pearson's r = 0.856, p=5.99×10−59; Figure 1—figure supplement 3) had more pups per litter (Figure 1F; β = 0.353, p=1.35×10−3, n = 328 litters from all breeding groups maintained in the same breeding facility; Supplementary file 3)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 1F

claim: For every additional centimeter of maternal body length, pup body mass increased by 2.9%.
source: Controlling for litter size, longer queens also had larger pups: for every additional centimeter of maternal body length, pup body mass increased by 2.9% (β = 0.29, p=0.032, n = 971 pups)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis controlling for litter size

claim: 171 genes showed a significant effect of breeding status at a false discovery rate threshold of 10% in the long bones.
source: Of 10,817 detectably expressed genes, 171 genes showed a significant effect of breeding status at a false discovery rate (FDR) threshold of 10% in the long bones (329 at an FDR of 20%; Supplementary file 4)
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq analysis

claim: No genes showed a significant effect of breeding status in the lumbar vertebrae at FDR thresholds of 10% or 20%.
source: Surprisingly, no genes showed a significant effect of breeding status in the LV at either FDR threshold
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq analysis

claim: Effect sizes were highly correlated between bone types overall.
source: However, effect sizes were highly correlated between bone types overall (R2 = 0.75, p=4.60×10−53)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of effect sizes

claim: Effects of breeding status were more pronounced in long bone samples than in lumbar vertebrae.
source: with more pronounced effects of breeding status in the long bone samples than in the LV (paired t-test on breeding status effects in long bone versus vertebrae: t = 3.97, df = 317.67, p=8.73×10−5)
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of effect sizes

claim: The majority cell type in both queen and nonbreeder samples was most similar to cells from the bMSC lineage.
source: Based on both canonical markers of bMSC lineage cells and deconvolution of the RNA-Seq data using data from 27 mesenchymal or hematopoietic lineage mouse cell types, the majority cell type in both queen and nonbreeder samples was most similar to cells from the bMSC lineage (Dominici et al., 2006; Hume et al., 2010; Newman et al., 2015; Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2)
evidence: Supported by cell-type deconvolution analysis and Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2

claim: The majority of breeding status-associated genes were upregulated in queens.
source: The majority of breeding status-associated genes were upregulated in queens (151 of 171 genes, 88%)
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq differential expression analysis

claim: Upregulated genes in queens were enriched for bone remodeling.
source: In support of their role in skeletal plasticity, upregulated genes were enriched for bone remodeling (log2[OR]=4.07, p=5.07×10−6), a process that involves the balanced cycle between bone formation by osteoblasts and bone resorption by osteoclasts (Redlich and Smolen, 2012; Figure 2)
evidence: Supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis and Figure 2

claim: Enriched pathways in queen upregulated genes were specifically related to bone resorption, not formation.
source: Surprisingly, however, enriched pathways were specifically related to bone resorption, not formation (Supplementary file 7), including 'positive regulation of bone resorption' (Figure 2A, C; log2[OR]=6.51, p=1.55×10−6) and 'superoxide anion generation,' which is involved in osteoclast activity and degradation of bone matrix (Figure 2A, C; log2[OR]=5.29, p=1.4×10−5) (Darden et al., 1996; Datta et al., 1996; Key et al., 1990; Key et al., 1994)
evidence: Supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis, Figure 2A and C, and citations

claim: Differentially expressed genes were enriched for immune-related processes.
source: Differentially expressed genes were also enriched for immune-related processes (e.g., 'cytokine secretion,' 'chemotaxis,' 'leukocyte activation involved in immune response'; Supplementary file 7)
evidence: Supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis

claim: Transcription factor binding motifs located in accessible chromatin near queen upregulated genes were enriched for PU.1 and MITF.
source: Specifically, transcription factor binding motifs (TFBMs) located in accessible chromatin near queen upregulated genes were enriched for PU.1 and MITF, two transcription factors that are essential for osteoclast differentiation (Segeletz and Hoflack, 2016; Figure 2B, C; PU.1 log2[OR]=1.041, p=2.84×10−4; MITF log2[OR]=0.707, p=7.36×10−3; see Supplementary file 8 for a complete list of enriched TFBMs)
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq analysis, Figure 2B and C, and citation

claim: No significant effects of estradiol treatment on gene expression were observed in either bone type.
source: Surprisingly, given the role of sex steroid hormones in bone growth and elevated estradiol levels in queen versus helper Damaraland mole-rats (Bennett, 1994), we observed no significant effects of estradiol treatment on gene expression in either bone type (all FDR > 10%)
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq analysis with estradiol treatment

claim: Queen upregulated genes were not in closer proximity to androgen response elements or estrogen response elements than expected by chance.
source: Queen upregulated genes were also not in closer proximity to androgen response elements (AREs) or estrogen response elements (EREs) than expected by chance (ARE log2[OR]=0.207, p=0.627; ERE log2[OR]=0.196, p=0.652)
evidence: Supported by analysis of proximity to hormone response elements

claim: Transcription factor footprinting analysis showed no evidence of queen-associated differences in transcription factor activity of AR, ESR1, or ESR2.
source: Consistent with this observation, transcription factor footprinting analysis showed no evidence of queen-associated differences in transcription factor activity of the androgen receptor (AR), estrogen receptor 1 (ESR1), or estrogen receptor 2 (ESR2), in either the long bones or LV (all paired t-tests: p>0.05; Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Supported by transcription factor footprinting analysis and Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: Breeding status could be predicted from morphological differences in LV6 with 77.8% accuracy.
source: We found that it could for the LV, but not for the femur: by applying the smooth Euler characteristic transform (Crawford et al., 2016), we were able to predict queen versus nonbreeder status in LV6 (77.8% accuracy, p=0.01, n = 36)
evidence: Supported by Euler characteristic transform analysis

claim: Breeding status could not be significantly predicted from femur morphology.
source: but not the femur (52.8% accuracy, p=0.53, n = 36)
evidence: Supported by Euler characteristic transform analysis

claim: Queens were less likely to have open growth plates in the proximal tibia compared to nonbreeders.
source: In the proximal tibia but not LV7, queens were less likely to have open growth plates (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 9; tibia: two-sided binomial test, p=0.019; LV7: two-sided binomial test, p=0.422)
evidence: Supported by histological analysis and statistical tests, shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Females with more offspring showed a higher expanse of closure across the growth plate in the tibia.
source: The increased probability of growth plate closure in the tibia of queens is linked to the number of offspring a female has produced: females with more offspring showed a higher expanse of closure across the growth plate (β = 0.050, p=4.51×10−3, n = 12, controlling for age)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of growth plate fusion

claim: Females that produced more offspring had fewer chondrocyte columns in the remaining growth plate.
source: This pattern may be due in part to reduced chondrocyte proliferation, as females that produced more offspring had fewer chondrocyte columns in the remaining growth plate (Figure 3D; β = −0.132, p=0.020, n = 12, controlling for age)
evidence: Supported by histological analysis and statistical test, shown in Figure 3D

claim: Cortical bone was significantly reduced at the femoral midshaft in queens compared to their nonbreeding sisters.
source: However, we found that cortical bone was significantly reduced at the femoral midshaft, but not in the LV, in queens compared to their nonbreeding sisters (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2; femur: paired t-test of cortical area (CA)/total area, t = −4.067, df = 8, p=3.60×10−3; LV6: paired t-test of CA/total area, t = −0.741, df = 6, p=0.487)
evidence: Supported by micro-CT analysis and statistical tests, shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: The femoral midshafts of queens showed significantly lower apparent density relative to nonbreeders.
source: Relative to nonbreeders, the femoral midshafts of queens showed significantly lower apparent density (paired t-test, t = −3.734, df = 8, p=5.75×10−3)
evidence: Supported by micro-CT analysis and statistical test

claim: Queens showed no difference in material density compared to nonbreeders.
source: but no difference in material density (paired t-test, t = −0.074, df = 8, p=0.943)
evidence: Supported by micro-CT analysis and statistical test

claim: Reduced bone mass in queens is due to reduced bone volume, not to reduced mass per unit volume.
source: Thus, reduced bone mass in queens is due to reduced bone volume, and not to reduced mass per unit volume (e.g., due to increased porosity)
evidence: Inferred from the finding that apparent density differs but material density does not

claim: Queens had a larger marrow cavity compared to their nonbreeding sisters.
source: Our analysis indicates that cortical bone loss in queens is due to the latter explanation: queens had a larger marrow cavity (paired t-test, t = 5.355, df = 8, p=6.82×10−4; Figure 3F)
evidence: Supported by micro-CT analysis and statistical test, shown in Figure 3F

claim: Queens showed no difference in periosteal area compared to their nonbreeding sisters.
source: but showed no difference in periosteal area compared to their nonbreeding sisters (paired t-test, t = 1.539, df = 8, p=0.162; Figure 3G)
evidence: Supported by micro-CT analysis and statistical test, shown in Figure 3G

claim: The relative amount of cortical bone in queens is not predicted by the number of pups in a queen's recent litter.
source: In support of this idea, we found that, within queens, the relative amount of cortical bone is not predicted by the number of pups in a queen's recent litter (pups born within the past 30 days; β = −0.024, n = 13, p=0.287)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: Queens who had more live births had reduced cortical bone thickness along the entire shaft of the femur.
source: Specifically, queens who had more live births had reduced cortical bone thickness along the entire shaft of the femur (Figure 4 and Supplementary file 10; across decile sections of the femur: all p<0.05, controlling for mother's litter as a random effect)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 4

claim: Cortical thinning does not commence with the transition to queen status per se.
source: Thus, cortical thinning does not commence with the transition to queen status per se (i.e., it is not a correlate of achieving breeder status), but instead appears to be a consequence of repeated investment in pregnancy and lactation
evidence: Inferred from the finding that cortical thinning is predicted by total offspring number, not recent litter size

claim: Thinning is particularly marked in queens who had at least six offspring.
source: Notably, thinning is particularly marked in queens who had at least six offspring, which usually occurs by 14 months after a breeding status transition (i.e., by the third litter; Supplementary file 10)
evidence: Supported by analysis of cortical thickness as a function of offspring number

claim: In nonbreeders, cortical area, minimum second moment of inertia, and polar second moment of area are positively correlated with body mass.
source: In nonbreeders, the three measures are positively correlated with body mass (CA: R2 = 0.409, n = 21, p=1.08×10−3; Imin: R2 = 0.412, n = 21, p=1.03×10−3; J: R2 = 0.422, n = 21, p=8.62×10−4)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: In queens, minimum second moment of inertia and polar second moment of area are not significantly predicted by body mass.
source: However, in queens, Imin and J are not significantly predicted by body mass (Imin: R2 = 0.088, n = 13, p=0.17; J: R2 = 0.239, n = 13, p=0.0514)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: In queens, minimum second moment of inertia and polar second moment of area are a function of number of offspring produced.
source: but are instead a function of number of offspring produced (Imin: R2 = 0.283, p=0.0354; J: R2 = 0.271, n = 13, p=0.0393)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: Queen cortical area is predicted by both offspring number and body mass, but offspring number explains almost twice the variance.
source: Queen CA is predicted by both offspring number and body mass, but offspring number explains almost twice the variance (offspring number R2 = 0.634, p=6.83×10−4; body mass R2 = 0.385, p=0.014)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: Cortical area is the best predictor of maximum load in mouse femurs.
source: In this data set, CA is the best predictor of maximum load (the maximum force a bone can withstand prior to failure), and, crucially, the CA-max load relationship is highly linear (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; R2 = 0.877, p=6.64×10−38)
evidence: Supported by citation to Jepsen et al., 2003 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Transitions to queen significantly increase the risk of bone failure.
source: Scaling the mole-rat CA data to mouse suggests that transitions to queen significantly increase the risk of bone failure (Figure 5; hazard ratio [95% confidence interval]=2.68 (1.18, 6.08), n = 34, p=0.018)
evidence: Supported by modeling using mouse data and Figure 5

claim: Queens who had at least six offspring showed the highest predicted risk of bone failure.
source: Similar to growth potential and cortical thinning, this effect is driven by highly fertile queens, such that those who had at least six offspring showed the highest predicted risk of bone failure (Figure 5; queens with ≥6 offspring relative to nonbreeders: HR = 3.74 (1.42, 9.82), n = 28, p=0.007)
evidence: Supported by modeling and Figure 5

claim: The risk of bone failure is predicted to increase by 21% for each additional pup.
source: The risk of bone failure is thus predicted to increase by 21% for each additional pup (HR = 1.21 (1.10, 1.33), n = 34, p=1.22×10−4)
evidence: Supported by modeling

claim: Vertebral lengthening observed in Damaraland mole-rat queens is concordant with previous reports in both Damaraland mole-rats and naked mole-rats.
source: The vertebral lengthening observed in Damaraland mole-rat queens is concordant with previous reports of vertebral lengthening in both Damaraland mole-rats (Thorley et al., 2018) and naked mole-rats (O'Riain et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citations to Thorley et al., 2018 and O'Riain et al., 2000

claim: Most growth in mole-rat queens is concentrated soon after the breeding status transition, especially in connection with the first post-transition pregnancies.
source: Like naked mole-rats, our analyses show that most growth is concentrated soon after the breeding status transition, especially in connection with the first post-transition pregnancies (Dengler-Crish and Catania, 2009; Henry et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by data and citations to Dengler-Crish and Catania, 2009 and Henry et al., 2007

claim: The growth phenotype in naked mole-rats occurs at the cranial end of the lumbar vertebrae.
source: for instance, while the growth phenotype in naked mole-rats occurs at the cranial end of the LV (Henry et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Henry et al., 2007

claim: The growth phenotype in Damaraland mole-rats is concentrated at the caudal end of the vertebral column.
source: it is concentrated at the caudal end of the vertebral column in Damaraland mole-rats
evidence: Supported by data showing differential growth in LV5 and LV6

claim: Damaraland mole-rats and naked mole-rats independently evolved a similar, highly cooperative social structure.
source: Given that Damaraland mole-rats and naked mole-rats independently evolved a similar, highly cooperative social structure (Jarvis and Bennett, 1993; Faulkes and Bennett, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Jarvis and Bennett, 1993 and Faulkes and Bennett, 2016

claim: The difference in location of vertebral growth between Damaraland and naked mole-rats suggests potential convergent evolution of the vertebral lengthening phenotype in queens.
source: this difference suggests potential convergent evolution of the vertebral lengthening phenotype in queens, presumably in response to the selection pressure for increased fertility
evidence: Inferred from the observation of similar phenotypes in independently evolved species

claim: Gene expression levels in queens reflect a signature of bone resorption, rather than bone growth, at the time of sampling.
source: Moreover, gene expression levels in queens reflect a signature of bone resorption, rather than bone growth, at the time of sampling, which occurred 1–2 years post-transition
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data showing enrichment of bone resorption pathways

claim: The molecular signature of bone resorption temporally aligns with changes in morphology.
source: The molecular signature of bone resorption temporally aligns with changes in morphology, in which accelerated vertebral growth primarily occurs during a female's first pregnancy, whereas cortical thinning in the long bones is a function of repeated cycles of offspring production
evidence: Inferred from the timing of gene expression changes and morphological changes

claim: Queens quickly progress from traits typically associated with pre-reproductive and pubertal growth to traits typically linked to aging.
source: Thus, queens quickly progress from traits typically associated with pre-reproductive and pubertal growth in mammals (e.g., body elongation), to traits typically linked to aging (e.g., marrow cavity expansion and cortical thinning)
evidence: Inferred from the observed sequence of morphological changes

claim: Estrogen levels are higher in mole-rat queens relative to nonbreeding females.
source: Because estrogen is known to impact bone growth and maintenance (Cutler, 1997; Khalid and Krum, 2016), and estrogen levels are higher in mole-rat queens relative to nonbreeding females (Bennett, 1994)
evidence: Supported by citations to Cutler, 1997; Khalid and Krum, 2016; and Bennett, 1994

claim: The results suggest a role for other, as-yet unknown signaling pathways in the queen-specific signature of long bone cortical resorption.
source: Thus, our results suggest a role for other, as-yet unknown signaling pathways in the queen-specific signature of long bone cortical resorption (although it does not exclude the possibility that estrogen signaling influences other phenotypes, such as bone elongation, growth plate closure, or collagen organization, which require further study; Juul, 2001; Cake et al., 2005; Ham et al., 2002)
evidence: Inferred from the lack of estrogen response in gene expression data

claim: Bone loss in Damaraland mole-rat queens may be an extreme of the typical mammalian pattern of bone remodeling.
source: Bone loss in Damaraland mole-rat queens may be an extreme of the typical mammalian pattern of bone remodeling, in which bone mineral density decreases during pregnancy and lactation, but recovers once offspring are weaned (Kovacs, 2016)
evidence: Speculative comparison to typical mammalian patterns, supported by citation to Kovacs, 2016

claim: Thinning in mole-rats may be sustained because queens can begin gestating soon after lactating for the previous litter.
source: Thinning in mole-rats may be sustained, however, because queens can begin gestating soon after lactating for the previous litter, leaving little to no time for recovery
evidence: Speculative explanation for sustained bone loss

claim: Queens in colonies with more helpers work less and rest more.
source: One possible reason that this fast rate of breeding is achievable is that queens in colonies with more helpers work less and rest more (Houslay et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Houslay et al., 2020

claim: Helpers might contribute to decreased bone mass in queens, given that reduced physical activity can lead to decreases in bone mass.
source: Paradoxically, helpers might not only help offset costs of, but also contribute to, decreased bone mass in queens, given that large numbers of helpers are themselves produced via high queen fecundity, and reduced physical activity can also lead to decreases in bone mass (Morseth et al., 2011)
evidence: Speculative reasoning supported by citation to Morseth et al., 2011

claim: In naked mole-rats, a small sample of queens suggests increased rather than decreased femoral cortical thickness relative to age-matched nonbreeders.
source: Similarly, in naked mole-rats (where colonies can include hundreds of animals compared to dozens in Damaraland mole-rat colonies; Jarvis, 1981; Jarvis and Bennett, 1993; Jarvis et al., 1994), a small sample of queens (n = 6) suggests increased rather than decreased femoral cortical thickness relative to age-matched nonbreeders (Pinto et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Jarvis, 1981; Jarvis and Bennett, 1993; Jarvis et al., 1994; and Pinto et al., 2010

claim: Abdominal lengthening allows queen mole-rats to increase fecundity per reproductive effort.
source: Specifically, while abdominal lengthening allows queen mole-rats to increase fecundity per reproductive effort
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between body length and litter size

claim: Loss of cortical bone in the femur is unlikely to directly benefit either fertility or survival.
source: loss of cortical bone in the femur is unlikely to directly benefit either fertility or survival
evidence: Inferred from the predicted increased fracture risk

claim: Loss of cortical bone reflects the cumulative burden of continuous cycles of pregnancy and lactation.
source: Instead, it reflects the cumulative burden of continuous cycles of pregnancy and lactation (Kovacs, 2016)
evidence: Inferred from the correlation with total offspring number, supported by citation to Kovacs, 2016

claim: Damaraland mole-rat queens incur morphological costs to concentrated reproduction in addition to morphological changes that facilitate increased fitness.
source: Thus, unlike eusocial insect queens (Rodrigues and Flatt, 2016; Rueppell et al., 2016), Damaraland mole-rat queens incur morphological costs to concentrated reproduction in addition to morphological changes that facilitate increased fitness
evidence: Inferred from the combination of beneficial (vertebral lengthening) and costly (bone loss) changes, supported by citations

claim: Queens gave birth to a mean of 6.92 ± 5.57 s.d. live offspring during the 12–22-month follow-up period.
source: Queens gave birth to a mean of 6.92 ± 5.57 s.d. live offspring during the 12–22-month follow-up period, produced in a mean of 2.85 ± 1.75 s.d. litters (range: 0–6; Supplementary file 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Helpers and solitaires produced no offspring.
source: As expected, helpers and solitaires produced no offspring
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Helpers and solitaires did not differ from each other in body mass or vertebral length after the 12–22-month follow-up period.
source: and did not differ from each other in body mass or vertebral length after the 12–22-month follow-up period (unpaired t-tests, all p>0.05; Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by statistical tests and Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Helpers and solitaires exhibited no differences in gene expression.
source: Because helpers and solitaires were morphologically indistinguishable, and also exhibited no differences in gene expression in our subsequent genomic assays (Supplementary file 2)
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq analysis

claim: Age at assignment was consistent with the age at dispersal observed in wild Damaraland mole-rats.
source: Age at assignment (mean age = 19.4 ± 4.4 s.d. months) was consistent with the age at dispersal observed in wild Damaraland mole-rats (1–3 years, Thorley and Clutton-Brock, unpublished data)
evidence: Supported by comparison to unpublished data on wild mole-rats

claim: The pairing procedure typically leads to immediate sexual activity and rapid activation of the reproductive axis.
source: This pairing procedure, which defines the queen treatment, typically leads to immediate sexual activity and rapid activation of the reproductive axis, including initiation of ovulation and the potential for conception (Bennett et al., 1996; Snyman et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bennett et al., 1996 and Snyman et al., 2006

claim: No effect of queen status on the amount of trabecular bone in the femur, tibia, LV6, or LV7 was found.
source: We found no effect of queen status on the amount of trabecular bone in the femur, tibia, LV6, or LV7 (all p>0.05 for bone volume/total volume)
evidence: Supported by micro-CT analysis

claim: The top three principal components summarizing estimated cell-type proportions did not differ between queens and nonbreeders.
source: Additionally, the top three principal components summarizing estimated cell-type proportions did not differ between queens and nonbreeders (all FDR > 10%, Supplementary file 5)
evidence: Supported by cell-type deconvolution analysis

claim: No cases were identified in which the effects of breeding status on gene expression were significantly mediated by the first principal component of cell composition.
source: and we identified no cases in which the effects of breeding status on gene expression were significantly mediated by the first principal component of cell composition (p>0.05 for all 171 queen-associated genes at 10% FDR; Supplementary file 6)
evidence: Supported by mediation analysis

claim: MITF was among the 151 genes that were differentially expressed between queens and nonbreeders and upregulated in both queen long bones and lumbar vertebrae.
source: MITF was also among the 151 genes that were differentially expressed between queens and nonbreeders and upregulated in both queen long bones and LV
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq differential expression analysis
